served.stem: A research assistant mixes 100 mL of a 25% sugar solution with 100 mL of a 10% sugar solution. What is the percent concentration of the mixture?

answer.line: 25 + 10 = 35 mL of sugar in 200 mL: 17.5 percent. Equal pours land halfway between 25 and 10.

steps: Count the sugar. 25 percent of 100 mL is 25 mL, and 10 percent of 100 mL is 10 mL: 35 mL of sugar.
Divide by the whole: 35 / 200 = 0.175, so 17.5 percent.
Check it with the seesaw. Equal pours balance in the middle, so here the plain average works: (25 + 10) / 2 = 17.5.

choices.note: 8.75 halves 17.5 again. Two 100 mL portions make 200 mL, so divide 35 by 200 once.
12.5 treats the 10 percent solution as plain water and halves 25. The second solution brings sugar too.
25 - 10 = 15 takes the gap between the strengths. A mix averages them.
35 is the milliliters of sugar. Divide by the 200 mL total to get the percent.

student.lockIt: Equal amounts mix to the plain average. Unequal amounts lean toward the bigger pour.

visual.alt: 200 mL splits into 100 mL at 25%, holding 25 mL of sugar, and 100 mL at 10%, holding 10 mL; together 35 mL of 200, 17.5%, outlined. On a seesaw from 10% to 25%, the two equal pours balance at the midpoint, 17.5, each 7.5 away.
visual.caption: Equal pours, equal weights: the seesaw balances halfway, at 17.5.
